speechtext:
Yesterday the member for Winnipeg North Centre asked two questions. First he asked why we proceed with this appointment by an act of parliament rather than, as the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act states in section 13, by a joint resolution of the House of Commons and Senate.
I am informed that in 1933, when the basic statute was passed, it stated that the auditors should be appointed by a resolution of parliament. The first appointment of an auditor under that act was in 1934, and the phrase "appointment by resolution of parliament" was considered. The law officers advised the government of that day that the only way the appointment could be made was by an act of parliament.
Without going into an elaborate explanation I draw to the attention of my hon. friend the debate of 1934, which is reported in Hansard. Then in 1936 the change I have outlined was made. Instead of using the phrase "resolution of parliament" it was changed to "joint resolution of the House of Commons and the Senate". However, by that time parliament had become accustomed to proceeding by way of a bill. This, as hon. members will appreciate, provides added control over legislation beyond what is provided in a resolution because a bill comes
1680	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways-Auditors to the members of both houses for attention more frequently than would be the case were we to proceed by a joint resolution. Therefore in consequence, despite that change in the statute in 1936, there has never been any change in procedure. We are today suggesting the appointment by way of an act of parliament just as has been done every year since 1934.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

Mr. Speaker, I thank the parliamentary assistant for going to the trouble to get the answers to those two questions which I put to him yesterday. It seems to me that the answer he has given to the second question is not only satisfactory but quite reasonable. I am, however, still interested in the answer given to the first question.
It seems to me that what he has said-if I may paraphrase it-is that the government is following custom rather than the statute. If it can be established, that the custom we are following is better than the provision laid down in the statute, it follows that it would be a good idea to amend the statute. Otherwise, does it not make a mockery of the rule of law and the importance of all of these fine details that we write into acts of parliament from year to year?
As the parliamentary assistant has pointed out, the wording that is now in the statute to which I drew his attention yesterday was put there in 1936. He admits that the statute was passed after the custom of doing it by act of parliament each year had been established. In other words, parliament knew what that custom was when it enacted in 1936 that it be done by a resolution of both houses in parliament.
As I indicated yesterday, in the end result there is no difference whatsoever. What we are talking about is not a matter of substance, and it is not even a matter of legality. It is a matter of procedure. In view of the importance that attaches to the laws that are passed by parliament and to the precise terms that are in them if it has been de-


cided to follow the custom rather than the law I suggest that at least the law might be changed to conform with the custom.

Mr. Speaker, I would refer you to a decision that you made on June 18, 1952, as reported at page 3375 of Hansard. I read these words:
After giving this matter my careful consideration I have come to the conclusion that if there is no objection to the consideration of the resolution in committee of the whole, the motion that the Speaker do leave the chair should be put without debate. It is in relation to that ruling that I propose to speak; and if the minister does not propose to speak, I shall go ahead.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend does so, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be desirable-on the point of order-that the whole of the extract to which he has referred
Emergency Powers Act should be put on the record. The paragraph immediately preceding the one which he read is as follows:
I should point out that the motion is for the Speaker to leave the chair, etc. It is not a motion to adopt the resolution. However, under our present practice members have been debating it as if it were such a motion. The minister makes an affirmative statement, frequently going into details, with the Speaker in the chair, and other members follow. The result is that a full discussion of the resolution takes place at this stage. I am sure that is not the procedure contemplated by standing order No. 60, nor is it in accordance with Mr. Speaker Glen's ruling, in which I concur.
It will therefore be seen that the Speaker's ruling which my hon. friend has invoked for the purpose he has in mind is dead against him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTINUATION OF ACT FROM MAY 31, 1953 TO MAY 31, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always extremely convenient to read the first part of a ruling and then say that the conclusion is against the position that is taken. I have read your conclusions, which you said had . been given to the house after careful consideration, and it is on the basis of that ruling that I am rising now to discuss the matter before the house.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the motion is that you leave the chair for the purpose of considering a certain resolution. In the case of emergency legislation of this kind, which is unusual legislation in this house, I submit that it is appropriate that we immediately decide whether we should take any steps at all to renew extraordinary legislation of the kind that we have had before us. I use the term "extraordinary" with the dictionary meaning of that word in mind. It is out of the ordinary to initiate proceedings designed to delegate to the executive the powers which are ordinarily exercised on behalf of the people of Canada by those who were sent here to do the business of parliament on behalf of those people.
The fact that we have already had an act of this kind in effect does not dispose of any of the objections to proceeding at this time to consider unusual legislation which confers upon the government the power to deal with almost every aspect of the life of the people of this country, subject only to certain reservations of a very limited nature. That surely is extraordinary legislation. Therefore I do submit that before we should even consider asking you to leave the chair for the purpose of having a discussion in regard to this, we should immediately place before the house reasons why no such steps should be contemplated at this time.
We are asked to say that you should leave the chair so that we may consider the desirability of introducing legislation similar to that which has been on the statute books

Emergency Powers Act now lor nearly two years. That legislation was passed over the objections of hon. members who pointed out that in the event that there should be a threat of general war, or such disturbance as might threaten the peace and security of the country, there was legislation already on the statute books under which the government could act at any time without waiting to convene parliament. Nevertheless this legislation was passed. It has been in force for nearly two years.
I submit that before a single step is taken to consider the reintroduction of legislation of that kind, we should ask ourselves today what evidence has come to us from the experience of the past few years which suggests any reason why we should suspend the ordinary authority of parliament in the way that is suggested by this resolution. It is not enough to say to hon. members that no injury has been done to the rights of parliament. I would contest that statement if it were made. I would concede, however, that the extent to which the wide powers of this act have been invoked is not sufficient to arouse any considerable concern in the minds of the public as to what the real effect of this act could be. We should be considering not what has happened but what could happen. We should consider the fact that while we are told from time to time that this government feels secure in office, conceivably another government may be in office while this act is still in force. That government also would have this act before it.
Legislation we pass must not be passed with the comforting assurance that the individuals who will be immediately entrusted with it can safely be given wide powers. We must see what wide powers are conferred and decide whether it is wise that any government at any time should have those powers. It is in that light that I think we should consider the proposal now before us.
We were told before in the preamble to the act which was adopted that an international emergency existed which threatened the security of Canada. No one can be in any doubt about that fact. One of the things which threaten Canada and every free nation of the world today is the loss of their personal freedom, which in our case is assured by our parliamentary democracy. For that reason we should be asserting the full authority of this parliamentary system of ours by the retention by parliament of its powers over the business of the people, at a time when the system itself is part and parcel of the struggle in which this whole world is engaged.

In the preamble to the act which will expire within the next few weeks it was said:
And whereas it is essential that emergency powers be conferred to enable measures to be taken as urgently required from time to time to carry out adequate defence preparations, to regulate the economy of Canada to meet the needs of defence and to stabilize the economy and to safeguard it from disruption that may result from defence preparation in Canada or from emergency measures taken in other countries, in order that defence preparations may not be impeded;
Then the act went on to say:
And whereas it is preferable that the necessary emergency powers be exercised under special authority from parliament rather than that the War Measures Act-
-therefore this act should be passed. What parliament was asked to do on that occasion, Mr. Speaker, was to pass an act which gave the government wide powers over the whole Canadian economy. These were the specific subject matters covered by the act:
(a)	control and suppression of maps, plans and photographs;
(b)	control of communications and means of communication;
(c)	control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada and the movements of vessels;
(d)	transportation by land, air or water and the control of the transport of persons and things;
(e)	trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture; and
(f)	imposition and recovery, in connection with any scheme of control, of fees or charges payable to the Receiver General of Canada or into any fund or account established by order or regulation for the purposes of the scheme of control.
Just let us think of what is covered by these words. First of all there is control and suppression of maps, plans and photographs. I am sure it will be said, "But that of course only means a limited type of photographs." The words are "maps, plans and photographs". Under this there is no limitation to the maps, plans and photographs that could be brought under the control of the government.
Indeed, that has already been held in the Nolan case, where the order in council obviously went far beyond anything that was contemplated when these emergency powers were originally conferred. The Nolan case, in fact, is a warning to us, and one of the reasons we should reconsider this matter carefully today. That case says in effect- and it will be kept in mind that it is a judgment of the privy council-that no matter how unrelated to the ordinary purposes of the measure itself the conduct of the government may be, if the government has decided that it will proceed under these emergency powers, that decision stands.

The judgment, in itself, is one reason we should pause today before making a single move to prolong extraordinary machinery which places in the hands of the government the power to deal with broad aspects of the economic and social life of this country, under the words I have just read in these various headings.
Let us think of what the government can control under the "control of communications and means of communication". That means that the ordinary communications between our people, one of the basic rights of a free people, could be stopped at any time. The courts, under the Nolan judgment, would be bound to say that no matter how far the government had gone, that order would stand.
Then we find that the government has "control of the harbours, ports and territorial waters of Canada and the movements of vessels." There again, under wide and unrestrained powers the government can control the operation of our harbours, our ports and territorial waters, and the movement of all the ships using them. These are powers so wide as to control the whole export business of this country, because it involves control over the movement of ships.
The next paragraph refers to "transportation by land, air or water and the control of the transport of persons and things". No wider power could be conferred. The whole movement of goods and of people is left completely under government jurisdiction and whim. They may make such decisions as from time to time they may regard as desirable, according to their idea of what is desirable.
Then we have the declaration that the government may control "trading, exportation, importation, production and manufacture". Mr. Speaker, this covers the whole economy of Canada. "Production" means production of all kinds. It means production by farmers; it means production by miners; it means production by forest operators. It means production of every kind from which the daily livelihood of our people is gained. And then, in addition to that, there is unlimited control over manufactures, which means the product of all the machines which give to our production in this country such tremendous scope and flexibility.
Then we have the declaration that it has all these wide-open powers, unrestrained by control, to determine how there will be "imposition and recovery, in connection with any scheme of control, of fees or charges payable to the Receiver General of Canada or into
Emergency Powers Act any fund or account established by order or regulation for the purposes of the scheme of control".
We were told, when this subject was discussed before, that there were exceptions which did leave the people with some possibility, some assurance, of freedom. That is in section 2 (2) of the act which reads:
Notwithstanding anything contained therein, the powers conferred on the governor in council by subsection one do not include power to make orders or regulations in relation to
(a)	arrest, except as incidental to proceedings under section three, detention, exclusion or deportation of any person;
(b)	censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings; or
(c)	expenditure of moneys otherwise than in accordance with an appropriation by parliament except expenditure of moneys from any fund or account established by order or regulation in connection with a scheme of control for the purposes of that scheme of control.
The exemptions and the protection here are almost illusory. "Censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings" seems to be a wide-open protection. It is a protection that certainly should exist, and that need not be discussed. But when we are told that the government protects the people of this country from arrest, let us see what it is in respect of which this protection is given. It protects the people from arrest, "except as incidental to proceedings under section 3". And section 3 provides that the governor in council may prescribe penalties-
*-by way of fine or by way of imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or by way of both fine and such imprisonment, that may be imposed for violation of orders or regulations made under this act and may also prescribe whether, and the circumstances in which, the said penalties shall be imposed upon summary conviction or indictment.
This simply means that, in relation to any of the subjects covered in section 2 (1), where the government makes regulations which must be observed in respect of any of these matters, if there is a breach of these regulations there may be arrest and all that follows arrest, without any restriction or any protection being afforded by section 2 (2) of the act.
1 can remember it was pointed out that no such wide powers as these had been exercised at any time. The suggestion was made that we need not be concerned about how wide these powers are because up to this time the government had not exercised such wide powers. In a very substantial measure that is so. Actually we are called upon to ask ourselves, before we take a single step in this matter, just why it is necessary that this should be done. Why are we asked to reintroduce an emergency

Emergency Powers Act act of this kind? What has the government found it necessary to do under the act which indicates a need for a continuance of its powers?
If the government is going to rest its case upon what it has done already, then let us see what it has done. These are orders passed under the act from May 1, 1952, to date, so far as I have been able to ascertain. First there is P.C. 2306, which was a consolidation of the previous regulations respecting great lakes seamen's security regulations. These regulations had to do with security on the great	lakes	and	the screening	of
seamen, with the declared intention of preventing communist activities in these very important operations.
The second order is P.C. 3197, passed on May 30, 1952. This was merely an order pursuant to the addresses of both houses which extended the act for a further year.
The third	was	P.C.	4116	passed	onSeptember 24, 1952. This was a partial revocation of	a previous	order	passed	on
September 26, 1951, respecting the power of the board of grain commissioners to defer the weighover at any terminal elevator.
Then there	was	P.C.	4410	passed	on
October 30, 1952, which was an order in council respecting pilots' licences under the Aeronautics Act and radio proficiency certificates under the Radio Act. These again ostensibly related to security and provided for the opportunity to screen those engaged in certain important activities.
No. 5 was P.C. 4525 passed on November 19, 1952. This was an order revoking previous order in council P.C. 1608, which provided the authorization for minting a new five-cent coin of steel. So far as I have been able to ascertain these are the orders in council that have been passed since May 1 of last year.
Let us see what this means. We may be told that it was not a very momentous order that was passed in regard to the five-cent piece. Let us be quite clear about it. It did not need any Emergency Powers Act to deal with that. Here was a subject that certainly called for no such wide powers. What was there relating to the world-wide tension or what was there relating to the threat from without and danger to our peace and security in the content of the five-cent piece? What was there that threatened the economy of Canada in the fact that there was steel in our five-cent piece at that time?
This does seem humorous, but the fact remains that the very absurdity of the proposition that this should be regarded as an emergency illustrates that this act is being used for matters that have nothing in the world to do with any such emergency as (Mr. Drew.]
was described in the preamble. This simply was a convenient way of dealing with something that the government decided was not important enough to bring to parliament. If the government really wants to tell parliament, "We do not think you should be bothered with ordinary details of this kind" then let them present a bill to us which will properly describe its real purpose. But do not come to us and say that you need an act based upon the presence of world-wide disturbances in order to deal with the Canadian five-cent piece.
Let us look at some of these other orders. One was simply an order implementing the recommendation of these houses that the act should be extended. However, there were two orders which I suggest should be considered. I believe that these orders are much more important than they appear on the surface. One was an order dealing with great lakes seamen's security regulations, and the other was an order in relation to the issuing of pilots' licences under the Aeronautics Act and radio proficiency certificates under the Radio Act.
The only reason for an emergency act is to have stand-by powers to deal with something that needs to be dealt with when events are crowding around in a way that make it impossible to wait for parliament to be convened in the ordinary way. The only justification for giving the government emergency powers at any time is that the very pressure of events, the demand for immediate action makes it essential that the government should not wait to convene the people's representatives to pass laws that would be required. No such emergency from that point of view arose in this case. In fact there was every reason why this act should not have been invoked for that purpose.
Over and over again the government has said that it was not prepared to deal with communist activities in this country by any law that would deal with those particular activities as such. Let us for the moment disregard the merits or otherwise of that argument. From the government's point of view, let us accept their contention. They say in effect, "You cannot define communism." They say in effect. "We must not under any circumstances exercise anything in the nature of thought control; we must not do anything that will impair the freedom of the individual to think and to express his thoughts." Having said that in the house and having refused to let parliament pass on laws which would define offences of this kind in the way they should be defined,

the government then say, "Although we cannot define the offence, we will not let people work because they have offended and are doing things that we cannot define."
Either there is an offence that can be defined, or there is not. If there is, it should be covered by our Criminal Code; if there is not, it should not be in the hands of this or any other government to deny to any Canadian or any other free citizen the right to work and maintain his family by his work.
This is not a case of the degree of confidence in the government. We would indeed he very strange on this side of the house if we expressed too unrestrained confidence in this government after some recent events. Nevertheless if we were in the unusual situation that notwithstanding all the disclosures there have been of the way in which this government has acted behind closed doors, we were prepared to say that this government is so good, this government is so reliable and this government is so efficient that we will delegate to the government all the powers conferred upon us under our constitution by the people of Canada, then I would say that we would be denying our right to sit here in this house of parliament if we said that this government at any time, secretly and without any definition of the offence, was going to be able to say to any individual whether or not he has the right to work. That is exactly what this means. That is exactly what these orders in council provide.
It is not enough to say to us, "You wanted action in regard to communism, and this is one way we can deal with it." If we are going to deal with communism-and I for one believe we should under laws which clearly define the offence, not under that name but under the nature of the offence-then I say that should be done by parliament and should be considered with the utmost care before the freedom of any individual is placed in jeopardy. Certainly there was no emergency of the kind described in the preamble which justified the use of this act in that way.
Then the other order in council was one which partially revoked an emergency powers order dealing with the handling of grain. Events are not yet crowding in around us in a way that denies us time in this parliament to deal with the way in which grain should be handled. Let the government bring before this house such legislation as is required to deal with grain of any kind or with other food products, and let this house determine what powers the government shall have to deal with matters of this kind.
Emergency Powers Act
The recital of the orders in council which were passed demonstrates perfectly clearly that during the past year the government did not need this act on a single occasion. It should not have used the act to deal with the subjects which are covered by the orders. Therefore the government themselves have demonstrated that during the past year, with all its international strains and pressures, they really did not need this act. What is there that they see looming ahead within the next few months that calls for the re-enactment of legislation of this kind? That is something that should be before the members of the house before we take a single step along the road of delegating our responsibilities to the executive.

Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this resolution is of great importance to the parliament of Canada and, more particularly, to the Canadian people. The issue raised by it is perhaps one of the most vital to be faced at this time.
I regret that although the resolution stands in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) he has not seen fit to make any explanation in opening the debate, and apparently is not greatly interested in the discussion. He may have appointments elsewhere, but I am sorry he is not in the house to hear the debate on this resolution which, I repeat, stands in his name.
I say the resolution is of great importance because it involves our whole structure of parliamentary government. As hon. members know, since 1914 we have had on the statute books of Canada a very unusual measure known as the War Measures Act. It became necessary to enact such legislation at that time, upon the outbreak of the first great war. It is not the kind of legislation liked in a country operating under a democratic system of government, because it gives far-reaching powers to the cabinet, as distinct from parliament.
In effect it takes away from parliament the right to consider a wide field of subjects. We all agree that it is the type of legislation which should not be used to any great extent. The act governs not only the eventuality of the actual outbreak of war, invasion or insurrection, but also covers apprehended war, invasion or insurrection. Action is taken under that legislation by the cabinet of the day sitting behind closed doors, with no opportunity for debate and very little opportunity for the public at large to keep in touch with what is enacted, which is one of the very serious objections to governing a country by order in council.
At the end of the war, in 1945, another measure was passed which was supposed to replace the War Measures Act which had been in effect by proclamation from early in September 1939 until this new legislation

Emergency Powers Act in the winter of 1945. The new act was known as the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, and came into force on January 1, 1946. It contained practically all the powers of the War Measures Act, and we understood at the time would be in effect for only a short time, until there had been an adjustment of the various problems brought about by the war. However it remained in effect until another act was passed, in 1947, known as the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act which was assented to on May 14 of that year and was to continue in effect until April 30, 1951.
That measure continued as law a group of orders in council which had been passed either under the War Measures Act or the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. When the bill was first introduced there were 57 orders in council listed in the schedule, and for that reason it became known as the Heinz bill. As it went through the house some of the orders in council were dropped but the bill still retained its name. As I said, it stood until 1951.
Then on March 21, 1951, another bill was assented to known as the Emergency Powers Act which has been in effect ever since. This resolution now before the house is asking for legislation which will continue the Emergency Powers Act in effect until May 31, 1954.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has pointed out already the powers given to the cabinet under the Emergency Powers Act, and I do not intend to repeat his statement in that regard. But I do point out that the powers contained in the Emergency Powers Act are nearly as far-reaching as those in the War Measures Act. When one examines carefully the terms one realizes that the Emergency Powers Act contains very far-reaching powers.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, to the house and to the Canadian people that the time has come to restore the supremacy of parliament. Let us put whatever powers are needed by the government on the statute books, rather than letting these powers be exercised by the cabinet sitting in secret behind closed doors and passing orders in council. Let measures be brought down in the ordinary way and be debated in this house. By the time a measure has been debated here most of the merits and failings will have been gone into pretty thoroughly, and each of us will be in position to know whether the legislation is good or bad.
This process of debate has another great value in that it is reported by the press gallery and distributed to all parts of the nation. The

people out in the constituencies are able to keep accurate track of what is being said in the house and thereby to judge for themselves the merits or demerits of a measure. I suggest that that is one of the strongest points in a democratic system of government. But you lose all that when you allow legislation to be enacted by order in council.
How many times were Canadians brought up in court and fined or sent to prison for failure to comply with the terms of an order in council about which they knew nothing. Time after time a man would be charged for a breach of some order or some regulation passed under the provisions of the War Measures Act or one of the acts which superseded it after the war. That Canadian in many cases had no chance at all to know whether or not he was breaking the law.

To get back to the point I was making, the privy council, when it referred to the economic power granted under the regulation, held as follows:
How, then, can a court of law decide that the vesting-
That is the vesting of property.
-was for another and extraneous purpose or hold that what the governor in council has declared to be necessary is not in fact necessary for the purposes he has stated? There is no warrant at all for presenting this as a case in which powers entrusted for one purpose are deliberately used with the design of achieving another, itself unauthorized or actually forbidden.
Then after finding that the court must accept what the order in council says, namely that there is an emergency, it finally says this at page 36:
For here the words that invest the governor with power are neither vague nor ambiguous; parliament has chosen to say explicitly that he shall do whatever things he may deem necessary or advisable. That does not allow him to do whatever he may feel inclined, for what he does must be capable of being related to one of the prescribed purposes, and the court is entitled to read the act in this way.
Then it goes on finally to say:
If rights so historic as a man's right to sell his labour where and at what price he pleases or a man's right to use his own property in his own way are avowedly placed under the governor in council as subjects of control and regulation, what peculiar sanctity can the law give to the ownership of consumable goods, so that this particular form of private right is to be exempted from any action in pursuit of the authorized purposes?
What it says finally is this:
Yet this is an enactment framed for the purpose of meeting an emergency that imperils the national life; it authorizes action over the whole economic field and extends to purposes outside the territory of Canada herself; it embraces purposes such as the maintenance, control and regulation of supplies, prices, transportation, the use and occupation of property, rentals, employment, salaries and wages, which have no meaning if they do not involve-
And I emphasize these words.
-a deliberate and consistent interference with private rights, including private rights of property. And the power of the executive to pursue these purposes, while the national emergency continues, is conferred by parliament without express reservation and in the amplest terms that statutory language can employ.
That is exactly the situation in the present legislation. When the present legislation was passed in 1951 the decisions of the courts
Emergency Powers Act were against the executive having these powers. The Manitoba case had been decided. When, on May 26, 1952, these powers were renewed in this parliament, the wording of the decision of the privy council was not before parliament and no hon. member had any conception of an interpretation such as that being given to the powers of the government.
This is a serious situation. When a government, power hungry in the days of war, persists in that attitude in the days of peace, the situation becomes serious indeed. The minister says now that the justification is the post-Korean situation. Well, if the postKorean situation has indeed created an emergency of a state of war, as the Prime Minister said the other day, then the legislation is not necessary. The Prime Minister said the other day that we are at war. If that is so, then the legislation is not necessary and certainly there can be no justification for the government asking for the abdication of parliamentary control and giving to the executive of this country the power to control every type of business in Canada, the power to deny an individual an appeal to the courts, the power to do absolutely that which parliament itself would permit only in the gravest situation and under the most serious conditions.

If the government is not prepared to accept a diminution of those powers, then, so far as parliament can achieve it, a stop should indeed be called.
Let me add this, that the use of powers asked for under this legislation would obviate the necessity of parliament's ever being convened during the period. We do not believe in a dictatorship. A book has just been published by a great British economist and political scientist, Professor Keeton, in which he points out that the elements of dictatorships are as follows:
1.	A one-party organization in which, although there is a wide power of criticism within the party, no external opposition is tolerated;
2.	An all-powerful executive, which can put into effect the program decided upon by the party, without substantial impediment or modification, especially that which might emanate from an independent parliament, and
3.	An economy which is moulded within the framework of a comprehensive plan, and in which all the more significant activities are government monopolies, subservient only to executive control.
All those things, with the exception of the first, are possible under this legislation. The minister says that powers have not been used during the last year. If they have not, and during the last year we have been in the post-Korean emergency to which he referred, what is the justification for their being asked for again, particularly in view of the judgment of the privy council?
Emergency Powers Act
These powers permit of rigid dictatorship within the periods between sessions of parliament. These powers constitute a denial of the rights of the individual under the powers of the constitution. These powers invade the rights of the provinces. These powers make the government-and by the government I mean the executive, the cabinet-all-powerful in the country. I feel that we in parliament have a responsibility to end this trend.
Two years ago the Prime Minister said that one of the reasons this legislation was to be introduced was to afford an opportunity to control inflation. There has not been any use of the powers for that purpose of which I am aware. The government has had within its own power the opportunity to do something. It could do it through a reduction of taxation. It could assure, in part, the defeat of inflation by encouraging production.
These are alternatives to the powers the government is asking under this legislation, powers that are available to a government that is prepared to act. I ask the minister to explain in detail why the government today finds it necessary to continue to disregard the constitution, and to destroy the rights of the provinces as effectively during the period this legislation is in effect as though section 92, which grants powers to the provincial legislatures, had no effect whatsoever.
Why these powers? How are they to be used? When are they going to be used? I would ask the minister once again to give consideration to what Professor Corry referred to in the reference I made a while ago in which he dealt with the setting up in parliament of a committee similar to that in the British parliament, whereby members of all political parties have placed before them in that permanent committee all regulations and orders passed that in any way derogate from the rights of the individual.
Surely that is not asking too much. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out that no lawyer in this country has any idea of the orders in council that have been passed, and that because of this he finds it difficult to advise a client. As a member of the House of Commons endeavouring to follow these orders in council, I can say that I have no conception whatsoever of many of these orders in council, and what they stand for. Those are the orders in council that we know of.
There are also orders in council that can be passed on the instruction or upon the suggestion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) or the Minister of Defence Production or whatever portfolio he may be described by at the moment. He

He can pass orders in council that place, above the courts of law, those who are favoured under the order in council. He can pass orders in council to preserve, from any liability before the courts, any company or person in Canada who is liable in damages for failure to carry out a contract in connection with defence production, and that covers almost everything.
I sum up. First, let us put an end to this trend. We know now where it leads. We know now that it places the government above the courts because the law officers word the orders in council wide enough to cover any eventuality. We know now that only the government through the governor in council can determine whether there is an emergency, and whether there is or not may not be examined by the courts. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has stated, by that fact parliament abdicates its responsibilities and the courts have become in effect, under orders in council passed under this legislation, merely instruments to determine rights, but are denied the opportunity to investigate whether or not property and civil rights may be invaded or the liberties of the subject interfered with. Keeton has summed up the situation in these words:
Behind the high sounding generalities of present-day politics, the issue is really a very simple one. It is whether we should accustom ourselves to the ant-like existence of the fully-integrated and planned state, or whether we believe that individual initiative and increased opportunity are more likely to produce more tolerable conditions of life for the bulk of our citizens. In the long run, it is impossible to preserve freedom of the mind when the power to choose has been removed from the citizen in more and more areas of his daily life. In the end, there will have been produced something approximating to the planned stagnation of the Chinese empire. That would be an odd fate for the people who built the common law and who were responsible for the Magna Carta, habeas corpus, and dominion status. Yet the threat is real, and the hour late. Our present predicament presents a challenge which it is impossible to ignore.
Surely parliament will not again in 1953 renew the grant of absolute power to a government now that the courts have determined that that government in the exercise of that power is above examination in so far as the determination of an emergency is concerned. If we adopt that attitude we in fact place the cabinet in the position of being restored to the same powers that cabinets had in the days of Sir Robert Walpole.

As a matter of fact, the need for it in terms of materials control, priorities and so on would seem to have lessened, if one can judge from the estimates in the Department of Defence Production and so on. But at any rate the plain fact of the matter is that the powers were not used for the purposes that we had in mind when we agreed to their extension; and it seems to us now that a government which certainly does not enjoy the confidence of a great many of us in this house, nor the confidence of the country, should not be given a further extension of powers of this kind.
I felt particularly proud of my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis)-I am always proud of him but I was particularly so today-for the reasonable speech he made earlier in this debate. From the way he spoke I think it was fairly clear that we were dubious about agreeing to this legislation. But despite that doubt, he left the door open and gave the government a chance to make a case for it if it had one. But despite that reasonable appeal-that reasonable offer-to the government to state its case, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) not only refuses to rise and do so but he rises and makes a speech on a point of order, thereby ruling himself out of court so far as his right to make any further speech on this matter is concerned.
I can tell the government that the slight doubt about this whole matter that we over here in this group had earlier this afternoon is no longer slight. We now feel that the issue is clear. We feel that what we have here is a government that wants wide powers, that does not want to explain why it wants them, that does not want to make a speech about the matter but just wants parliament to agree to the extension of these powers. To say that they were passed last year or the year before is hardly an argument. It might have been a point for the minister to make if he had spoken first.

But after five or six members of the opposition have spoken and have indicated disagreement with this legislation, surely the time has come for the government to make a case for this legislation, if it has one; and I greatly doubt that it has.
As I have already said, even if it had a *case, any confidence that any of us ever had in this government is completely gone, and we have no thought of giving them powers of this kind.

The members of the government still think they have the confidence of the people of this country. There is one way they can find out, and they will be very surprised when they make that test.
One of the reasons I was hoping we would have a speech from the government side before this-after all, I am the sixth speaker on this side and there has been no word from the government yet-was so that we might have a summary of what has been done, if anything, under the Emergency Powers Act during the last twelve months. A year ago-in May, 1952, it was-when the house was asked to extend this legislation, the Prime Minister gave us a report of the government's stewardship under this legislation. He told us how many orders in *council had been passed under the Emergency Powers Act. He described each of them. At least, he described all but one of them, and I will come to that matter in a moment. But at any rate we were given an account of what had happened during those twelve months. I should like to know whether more or fewer orders in council were passed this year than were passed last year under the Emergency Powers Act. Some questioning took place a while ago. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) wanted to know. whether the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) knew how many orders in council had been passed under this legislation during the past five years. That was an odd question because this legislation has not been in effect for the last five years; it has been in effect for only two years.
Emergency Powers Act
I may say that during the first year there were, in fact, only nineteen orders in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act. I am referring to the year from 1951 to 1952. The Prime Minister detailed those for us *last year. As I say, he told us that there were nineteen. Of those nineteen, fourteen were still in effect when the Prime Minister spoke to us on May 26, 1952. Those fourteen were as I shall now indicate.
There were five dealing with great lakes seamen's regulations, three having to do with priorities control, two with respect to control of transport, one that had grown out of the foot-and-mouth disease, one that had to do with the operation by United States government agencies of radio stations within Canada, and one that had to do with the exempting from customs duty of gifts having a value of less than $25 if sent home by troops overseas. I think the figures I have given add up to thirteen. The other one of those fourteen which was still in existence a year ago was P.C. 3486 of July 4, 1951, which, by government decision, had been exempted from publication. In other words, that is a secret order in council, the terms of which parliament does not yet know.
In addition to those fourteen that were still in effect when the Prime Minister spoke on May 26, 1952, there were five others. Obviously some of those fourteen may since have been repealed or rescinded. Incidentally this is the kind of information that I think the house was entitled to have if the government had not followed the insulting course to which we have been subjected today.
With respect to the other five I may say that the Prime Minister a year ago, at the time he spoke, indicated that those five had been replaced by legislation, or by proper statutes. One of them had to do with the Defence Services Pension Act; another had to do with discipline in the armed forces. A third one had something to do with the agricultural products board. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is good at getting things done when he wants them done- except the South Saskatchewan dam. A fourth one had to do with the use of other metals than nickel in the Canadian five-cent piece. It is not worth much any more anyway. The last one had to do with the postponing of the weighing of grain under certain conditions.
I recite those nineteen orders in council, fourteen that were still in existence and five that had been replaced, not just to put a bit of history on the record but to indicate the kind of use that was made of this legislation,
1706	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act in the light of such information as we had been given up to that time. The last five orders in council that I referred to were certainly not emergency matters at all. As a matter of fact they were all just cases of the government's using the Emergency Powers Act as a convenience, as a means of getting something as law before parliament would pass the actual legislation. As to the other fourteen, with respect to some of them-for example, the one having to do with the foot-and-mouth disease-the Prime Minister admitted that there was probably other statutory authority, that they really did not need to use the Emergency Powers Act. So when you add it all up, it looks as though the use of the Emergency Powers Act during its first year was simply a use for convenience, and that there was little done that was in terms of security. One does not know, of course, what was in that secret order in council of July 4, 1951; but in the main it was simply a matter of convenience to the government during that first year to have this legislation on the statute book. I suggest that we should have been told before this what the story has been during the second year. How many orders in council have there been? Were there more than nineteen? Were there fewer than nineteen? Incidentally, hon. members must not get the impression that the government holds itself down to nineteen orders in council a year. Those are just the orders in council under the Emergency Powers Act. That does not include the orders in council that come under the legislation over which the Minister of Trade and Commerce and of Defence Production is in charge, and it does not include orders in council under all the other pieces of legislation, most of which make provision for some form of order in council or other.
As hon. members know, we get a book every once in a while containing orders in council that have been made and tabled in the house, and to keep up with them would require quite a secretariat indeed.
What has happened during the past year? Have there been any that could not have been effected under other legislation? Have there been any in connection with which the purpose could not have been served by legislation of this parliament? After all, we are here most of the year now. There is not ever a very long break between sittings of parliament, and if the government really believed in parliamentary democracy, in parliament being in charge rather than just the executive, I do not think they would have asked for this kind of legislation at all. As the hon. member for Kamloops reminds


me, if they believed in responsible government, which is supposed to be the essence of our form of government, our form of democracy, I do not think they would be asking for any further extension of this legislation.
It may be argued that the world situation is still a precarious one, and no one would deny that. Some of us are quite concerned about some of the things that are happening, even happening in the country to the south of us, in terms of changes in foreign policy, and we do not know just what may be ahead; but in that connection may I remind the house that when the Prime Minister introduced this legislation on February 20, 1951-it was the occasion when we were at the same stage that we are at now, only on that occasion the Prime Minister chose to speak -he said, as reported at page 497 of Hansard:
Moreover, the enactment of an emergency powers bill will not prevent the proclamation of the War Measures Act if the situation should become more critical than it is now.
He went on to say-and I read this because it has a bearing on the sentence I have just read:
Of course it would not prevent the proclamation of the War Measures Act if we got into a state of actual conflict.
The Prime Minister was saying there what we all know that in a state of actual conflict there is nothing to prevent the government from proclaiming the War Measures Act. The Prime Minister went further than that on February 20, 1951. He said that if conditions became more critical than they were then, but even short of actual conflict, it would be possible for the government to proclaim the War Measures Act. Well, so long as the government has that residual power, that residual right to proclaim the War Measures Act, it could deal with anything that was a real emergency, and therefore I do not see why it should ask for the continuance of this legislation any longer. It is convenient for the government to have this legislation, I know, and they like to get things through in the easiest possible way. To pass an order in council in cabinet meeting over in the east block is much easier than getting a bill through this House of Commons, but surely that should not be the basis on which decisions of this kind are made.
We feel-I think it could be said even of this government

that they would be a bit reluctant to proclaim the War Measures Act in any situation that was short of actual conflict. With respect to the relationship between parliament and the executive I think it is good for that reluctance to be there and for the government to be held in check to that extent. So long as they have not

got the War Measures Act they will be careful; they will come to parliament more often. But if they get this Emergency Powers Act before them it is obvious from their record that any time they get into a little jam, any time they want to put something else into the five-cent piece besides nickel, any time the Minister of Agriculture wants a change in one of his pieces of legislation, any time you need to amend legislation that you want changed when parliament is not here, well you just pass an order in council under the Emergency Powers Act and that will do the trick until parliament gets back to pass legislation. Well, that is playing fast and loose with the whole set-up of parliamentary and responsible government, and for my part, though we gave the government these powers two years ago and extended them last year, the plain fact of the matter is they have not used them for the purposes that some of us had in mind when we gave those powers. Rather, they have used them just as a convenience, and I do not think they should have them any more.
I do not know what the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) had in mind when he asked as to the number of orders in council that had been passed under this legislation. I do not know whether the Minister of Justice was prompting him or not, whether he was hoping to get out the information that there had not been very many. That may well be the case. I do not know. It may well be that there were fewer than nineteen in the past year, which was the number the year before. If that is so, if there were very few occasions on which it has been necessary to use this legislation, I would suggest that it should be abandoned because of disuse, because having it there as a convenient piece of machinery that the government can use is bad for democracy and bad for relationships between the executive and parliament. We have had those bad relationships not only in terms of the legislation itself, we have had a terrific example of it today in the way in which the government has dealt with this matter, and in my view parliament should not consent to the passing of the motion for Your Honour to leave that chair.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you would call it six o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, before I conclude my remarks at this stage of the debate 68108-109
Emergency Powers Act I feel the house should be given a picture, in capsule form if possible, of what has happened to date.
There was moved this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a resolution that stands on the order paper in his name. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) asked if there was not going to be a statement from the government at this stage, whereupon the Prime Minister said that he believed the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) had a statement to make. The Minister of Justice interjected to say he preferred to make his statement in committee of the whole.
The Leader of the Opposition pressed the point that this was a matter of some importance, and that he felt there should be a statement with Your Honour in the chair. Despite that urging on the part of the Leader of the Opposition the Minister of Justice chose not to speak at that stage, nor did anybody else from the government side of the house offer to speak.
There followed the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and then the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). That made four speeches from the opposition side of the house, all more or less opposing the motion that Your Honour leave the chair for the house to go into committee of the whole on this particular resolution,
At this point-and I am relying upon my memory, but I am prepared to subject what I am saying to the reading of Hansard when it comes out tomorrow-at that point the Minister of Justice rose and started to speak. He said something like this, "Mr. Speaker, if all those who have any objections to raise have stated them, I feel it is my duty to reply". I place emphasis upon the word "duty" which the Minister of Justice used at that time.
In other words he was at that point prepared to follow up the suggestion made by Your Honour in 1952 that, there having been speeches directed to the negative of the question on a motion of this kind, it was his duty and responsibility as a minister to reply. I rose on a point of order to make sure the Minister of Justice did not presume that he was closing the debate. He replied that he certainly was not closing the debate. He said that he was rising on what really was a point of order to make sure that there were not others who wished to speak in opposition to the motion because, as he said-and I remember this particularly well-"I do not

Emergency Powers Act want to be put in the position where I cannot answer objections that are raised against this legislation".
When from this side of the house we made it clear that there were others who did wish to speak, the Minister of Justice took his seat. For a moment it looked as though the question was going to be put. Some of us complained that it would be an insult to this House of Commons if the matter were concluded without a speech from the government side of the house. The Minister of Justice still sat in his seat.
There followed then the speech of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). When he finished, again there was silence from the government side, and Your Honour was about to put the question. At that time I asked if the Minister of Justice was not going to make a statement. He got up and said that he was rising just to speak briefly, to explain why it was his intention not to speak at that stage. Well, his brief remarks were not exactly brief; and at the end of his remarks Your Honour took the position that the length at which he had spoken, and the extent to which he had dealt with the substance of the matter, made his remarks a speech, and that therefore he would not be able to speak again in this debate.
In other words at that point the Minister of Justice did the very thing that earlier he said he did not wish to happen. Earlier he had said, "I do not want to be put in a position where I cannot reply to objections to this measure", and then a little later on he put himself in the very position that he said he did not want to be put into.
So the result is that, not counting the speech made by the Minister of Justice- because he did not deal with the merits or demerits of the proposal before us and therefore it should not be counted-there have been six of us, including myself, who have taken part in the debate, and all of us on the opposition side of the house. All of us have expressed either misgivings or outright opposition to the measure.
I suggest that this is a very strange situation indeed. This afternoon I used words which I thought at the time maybe were strong; but, on thinking it over, I am satisfied those words were quite proper, and suited the situation. It seems to me that the government is insulting parliament by asking us to agree to legislation of this kind without even making any statement as to why parliament should be asked to vote for this measure.
I indicated this afternoon that a year ago the Prime Minister did not hesitate to tell us why he thought parliament should agree


to the extension of the Emergency Powers Act for another year. I even gave some of the details that were in that speech-details of a kind to which I think we are entitled on this occasion. So far today we have had no explanation at all, and it simply leaves us on this side of the house with the feeling that we have here a government which is not only seeking wide powers and seeking to have parliament delegate parliamentary authority to the executive, but wants that to be done without even telling parliament why, in the government's opinion, it should be done.
I suggest as strongly as I can that the reference to rules and to points of order is irrelevant. If this debate were out of order Your Honour would not let it -carry on. There is no question as to our right to speak, and there is no question as to the right of members on the government side of the house to speak as well. As a matter of fact, since so much has been said about the rules in the book, may I remind hon. members of citation 214 in Beauchesne's third edition which suggests that His Honour the Speaker is supposed to alternate speakers between the two sides of the house. Well, we cannot but sympathize with Your Honour today owing to the fact that nobody on the other side has tried to speak. And so Your Honour has had to see a succession of speakers on the opposition side.
The suggestion has also been made that members on the other side of the house are just following the rules. Well, standing order 38 makes it clear that this is a debatable motion. Standing order No 60, to which reference has been made so often, does not preclude debate at this stage. It says that before a motion of this kind can be dealt with it must be referred by the house to a committee of the whole house, and it is clear from standing order 38 that a motion to refer this matter to a committee of the whole house is a debatable motion. It is that right that we are exercising at this time. As I said this afternoon, the government may argue all it wants that what we have before us now is simply a motion that Your Honour get out of the -chair, but everyone knows that if this motion were defeated the government would not treat it as a defeat of a procedural motion; the government would say that what the house had done was to deny any further consideration of a major government proposal.
This is a major proposal; it was included in the speech from the throne. It is before us as a substantial proposal in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and I am satisfied that if the house were to stand

on its rights as a free parliament in a democracy that believes in the parliament of Canada being superior to the executive branch, if taking that position this house were to defeat the motion that Your Honour leave the chair, that would be correctly and properly interpreted as a defeat of the proposition that is before us, namely, that the Emergency Powers Act be extended for another year.

Mr. Speaker, if I believed that this question was simply one of procedure I would hardly have the heart to stand up and talk on the subject because I believe there are those who are much more familiar with constitutional and procedural matters than I am. But it does not seem to me to be that at all. As I understand it, it is really a question of the cutting down of the rights of the minority in this house. I am not able to see it in any other way.
I understand that we have heard questionings of the practice which has prevailed during the few years I have sat in this house. It has been questioned once or twice. As I see it now, we are having the matter pressed. The minister is refusing to take part except 68108-109i
Emergency Powers Act in the procedural sense in this resolution stage. To me this is a shrinking of the rights of the minority and it is because of that that I am on my feet.
I have always been most interested in the ample rights of debate that are given to the minority under our system. It seems to me to be evidence of the great wisdom of our ancestors. I have not been able to find anyone who could enlighten me in detail as to the way it arose. There is one interesting suggestion which was made to me once and which I have always carried in my mind, that perhaps it went back to the time when members of parliament had retainers at home, not in the legal sense, but men-at-arms, and it was considered better to give them ample rights of speech rather than have them go back home and perhaps put the matter to a very different test.
Whatever the rights may be that we have had under our system, the rights of the minority are certainly very amply protected. My own feeling is that that is of vast importance. I have often asked myself why it is that only the countries that share our form of government, and perhaps not all of them, are prepared every few years to have the citizens of the country put pieces of paper in boxes all across the country and at the end of that time obey, because that is what we do, the people who have the largest number of votes.
The results are often very unsatisfactory to us. They have been most unsatisfactory to me for a long time. Nevertheless one obeys the results, and I suggest we do that for two reasons. First, I think we like to think that we are sporting people and when we are defeated we like to take it in good part. But far more important than that, I believe, is the fact that we feel that the rights of the minority will be protected, that there will be ample opportunity for them to be voiced. Therefore I feel that any attempt of any kind to cut them down should be resisted, and that is the reason why I am on my feet.
I have found something that I have looked for for a long time, a short description of minority rights, rationalizing them better than I have ever seen them rationalized, showing why the rights of the minority are as amply protected under our system as they are. Before I read this may I say that although they are amply protected I cannot from my short experience feel that there has been very great trespassing. I cannot feel that time has been lost.
There have been very few cases when we have had what we might call a textbook illustration of the success of the opposition

I am hoping that Mr. Speaker will think it is relevant to what I am trying to point out, namely, the rights, the privileges and the effectiveness of the opposition. When I have read the short passage which I propose to read I believe the Minister of Public Works will think it is relevant. At any rate I shall be very brief.
What happened then was that we in the opposition exercised our duty of protesting. We were fortunate in that case in that we attracted the attention of the press and the matter became of public interest. We are not always so fortunate in that way. The minister will remember that within two weeks the government for once saw the light. They saw that we were right and the measure was halted. I mention that because it is the clearest illustration I can think of of one of the reasons for the existence of the opposition.
I propose to read shortly from "The Procedure of the House of Commons" by Redlich, volume I, page 131. It seems to me that this sets out extremely well what an opposition is for. I quote:
As already pointed out, the distinctive characteristic of the procedure finally developed in the 18th century was the protection of the minority. This principle also can only be understood as one of the consequences of the cohesion which has marked the House of Commons since the revolution.
Note this carefully, Mr. Speaker.
The opponents who face each other are equally able and willing to undertake and become responsible for the government of the kingdom;-
Of course that is not something which we all agree with, but that is what the text writer says.
-more than this, they are ready to recognize each other's capacity.
He may be going a little far there.
The prospect of loss of power awakens in the hearts of the ruling party no fear of destruction for themselves and no fear of an attack upon the constitution for state and country. The battle is one upon an enclosed field. It is, therefore, quite in place that there should be rules of battle to assure fair play to each party. For both are members of a nation, one in fact and feeling. The majority holds the great advantage of being able to realize its wishes in the institutions of government; but, on the other hand, for this very reason


the minority ought to have all conceivable rights of expressing its views and aims, and ought to be allowed free use of all permissible weapons of speech and political tactics in its fight against the expression of the wish of parliament which is a consequence of possessing a majority. For it is just as much the interest of the nation to ascertain whether the majority can maintain itself as such against an able and powerful attack and make proper use of the great privilege of conducting the government, as it is to take care that the will of the ultimate majority shall be treated as the will of the nation.
Then there is this final sentence, Mr. Speaker, which reads as follows:
Protection of the minority is, therefore, in the British parliament no mere privilege of the minority for the time being; it is a vitally important institution developed in the highest interests of a nation ruled by parliament.
I have no doubt that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will say that he endorses all that and that nothing he is doing today contravenes that in any way. All I can say is that there we differ entirely. I feel that this is one of the instances we see so often where a little tenure of power makes power commonplace. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) smiles. He is not hearing this for the first time and its amuses him greatly, but nevertheless I do not hesitate to reiterate it because signs are never wanting that that is what happens, that when people have it for a long time they come to have complete confidence in themselves and they come to be completely convinced that more and more power for them is better and better for the nation. I do not like to say that in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He of course is an authoritarian.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce, who calls a spade a spade, referred once to having power. He said it was useful to have a stick or a club behind your back when you were negotiating with anyone. In any event, as I understand it there is a stand-by, the War Measures Act, which could be proclaimed and which could do the job if it were necessary. It seems to me we have about reached the situation where these emergency measures should only be used in case of a clear emergency and not in the somewhat nebulous condition in which we find ourselves now. If I remember right, the government hesitated to act on grounds of emergency the other day, saying that there was not one, and now we are asked to pass legislation on the ground that there is one.

It seems to me that we got along very well with the procedure that was used in my early years in this house, and then it suddenly seemed to become unpopular on the other side of the

Emergency Powers Act gangway. Today we are witnessing a definite attempt to adopt an attitude of insistence. I still hope that the Prime Minister will speak and that we may have a complete reversion to the system which seems to me to have served us so well.

I might just point out to my hon. friends on the other side of the house that they have not shared your generosity, Mr. Speaker, because although you have been prepared to accord me an opportunity of answering, they seem to have been somewhat indisposed to hear the reply. This resolution has been before the house since three o'clock this afternoon. From that time multitudinous opportunities have been afforded the Prime Minister or any other minister on the government side to explain why it is expedient that this resolution be passed, and why it is desirable that the Speaker leave the chair. He and they have all carefully refrained from exposing themselves to the obvious weakness of their own case by attempting to undertake an explanation of the desirability of that move.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that when the Emergency Powers Act, which is the subject of the resolution before the house, was introduced in 1951 it was passed, with reservations, but generally speaking with the consent and approval of the house. February 1951, it is well to recall, was only eight months after Korea, and no one knew just what Korea would bring. No one knew whether it would extend to become a world-wide conflagration, whether in fact it would become that national and international emergency which at that
Emergency Powers Act time was the fear, whether expressed or not, which was in the minds of all members of this house and the people of all the peace-loving nations. We felt there was some justification for the introduction by the government of a bill, of which the title was the Emergency Powers Act, the act which it is now desired to extend for a further year by a bill to be based on this resolution if this resolution passes.
But I submit to you, sir, and to the whole house, that although there was justification for the qualified support of the resolution and the bill in 1951, there is no such justification for supporting the resolution before the house today. There are various reasons why that is so. The first reason is that the government has not, in any sense whatever, attempted to define either the emergency, by virtue of which it is seeking these powers, or the spheres within which these powers will be exercised. Not only that, but as was pointed out on several occasions this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), they have not used the powers in very many cases, although in many of the cases in which they were used they were used in respects of which it was entirely unnecessary to rely on emergency powers and what they did might far better have been done by ordinary legislative process. But now it is becoming increasingly obvious that the government, finding these emergency powers more and more of a convenience, are simply expecting the House of Commons to extend those powers without the slightest effort on their part to explain to the house why it should continue to surrender its control over legislation-which it is the task and part of parliament to exercise-into the hands of the executive. We are now being asked to pass this bill extending these emergency powers for a further year without one word of explanation.
Your Honour has indicated that it is perhaps not germane to the subject matter of the resolution before us to dwell at any greater length on the fact that the Prime Minister, who introduced it, does not even consider it appropriate to explain to the house why he thinks it is expedient that this legislation should be considered. I will not deal with that matter at any greater length; but I think it should be emphasized and should at all times be within the knowledge of every member of the house, and of every person throughout the length and breadth of this land, that the government which is asking this parliament to surrender for a further year its legislative responsibilities and control of the executive is asking that parliament do
