Emergency Powers Act so without even the gesture of affording us one word of explanation as to why it is necessary to carry on that system.
Mr. Speaker, the situation which confronts this house and this country today is a vastly different one from that which confronted us when the Emergency Powers Act was first enacted by parliament two years ago. It is true that the situation in Korea is not settled by any means. There exists a state of war in Korea. Incidentally, it has taken considerable prodding and pressing on the part of members on this side of the house to persuade the government to admit that the situation amounts to a state of war. They used to call it "police action", as you will remember, until they found it rather inconvenient to explain it on that basis to the people of Canada whose families were disrupted and whose pockets were plundered by the taxes supposed1 to be made necessary for this thing. They found it rather hard to justify all those things by the term "police action".
It is true that we have a state of continuing war in Korea. But with regard to that situation the uncertainties which were present in February, 1951, only eight months after the war broke out there, are not now nearly as vague, indefinite or threatening as they were then. A method of dealing with that situation seems to have been contrived on the part of the peace-loving nations of the world. We must remember that not only is the situation far different in all respects from the uncertainties of the one which surrounded the outbreak of the Korean war, but that just recently in this house, in connection with another measure and in a discussion with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) as to the question whether or not an emergency existed, the Prime Minister said: After all, these matters are not so much matters of difference in definition as they are matters of difference in degree.
What, therefore, are we left with as a justification for the continuation of this measure? We are left with nothing more or less than the fact that the government is to say whether or not it thinks the emergency to be of a sufficient degree-not by definition but of a sufficient degree-to warrant parliament's continuing to abdicate all its legislative functions and all its legislative responsibilities. Yet although they say that the decision whether or not parliament should continue to be deprived of its legislative responsibilities and functions depends upon whether or not the emergency is of a sufficient degree to warrant it, they have the supreme effrontery this afternoon to introduce 

this resolution saying that we should continue to abdicate our responsibilities, without even the gesture of an attempt to explain to us what is the degree of the emergency upon which alone the Prime Minister said, some three days ago, justification for this or similar measures would depend.
First he tells us that the existence or otherwise of an emergency is a matter of degree and that it depends upon the determination of the government as to whether the necessary degree of emergency exists. Now he comes along and says "We are asking you to continue the emergency legislation", and he has the supreme effrontery to ask the Canadian people in their parliament to do that without getting up and saying what is the degree of emergency upon which he bases the request for a continuation of this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, never could there have been clearer proof of the fact that this legislation should no longer be continued and that this government should be brought to a realization of its responsibilities not only to this house but to the people of Canada, and its responsibility to explain fully-if indeed it is possible to explain-why the parliament of Canada should continue to be deprived of its legislative authority, of the means by which -and by which alone-that parliament and thus the people whom the members of parliament represent can control the executive branch of the government, namely, the cabinet.
Until that explanation is given I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to every hon. member in this house, that we would be completely lacking in the discharge of our duties as individual members representing our constituents and the people of Canada as a whole if we were to abdicate, without a word of explanation or justification, the very duties which those people sent us down here to discharge, namely the duty of investigating, controlling, checking and, if necessary, denying the measures which the government submits to us. After all, that is the supreme function of parliament and it is the supreme task of every member of parliament to exercise his judgment on behalf of the people whom he was elected to represent. If we simply refuse to allow ourselves for a moment even to be in a position to exercise that judgment, then we betray the confidence which the people who elected us placed in us when they sent us down here.
Hence, not only do I say that this resolution should be defeated because of the complete lack of explanation and the complete lack of justification which has been afforded to us as to why the Emergency Powers Act should

be continued; but indeed, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that the words of the Prime Minister himself, when he was speaking to the house in support of the bill in March, 1951, contained-if anything further were needed-an additional reason why the legislation should not be continued. The Prime Minister, when he spoke in support of the legislation in 1951, made it perfectly clear that it went far beyond what the government thought might be necessary. He came before parliament and he said: We are asking you to pass legislation which confers upon the government the power to enact, by order in council, all these things which normally would require the authority of parliament through a statute. Not only that, but also we are asking you to empower the governor in council to do things in fields which would normally be reserved exclusively to the provinces.
He said: We are asking you to give us these powers, but we are not asking you to confine these powers to fields and within limits within which we ourselves are prepared to say in detail that we need those powers; we are also asking you to entrust to us powers which might be far wider than anything which we ourselves can foresee that we shall need. That is what he said to us in March, 1951. I cite in support of that paraphrase of the Prime Minister's remarks this passage from page 807 of Hansard of March 1, 1951:
These things mean restrictions on some individuals and they are subject to contestation before the courts. It is therefore important to have the language so broad that the courts will not say: "You have gone beyond what parliament authorized you to do." I am sure there is contained here a good deal that goes far beyond what will be done by order in council or by regulation. But the Department of Justice feared-at least, that was the advice we obtained from the permanent officials-that if it was not drawn in the broad language that already had had the scrutiny of the courts and had been upheld by the courts, they would not guarantee that it would stand contestation. We were convinced that we should stay on the safe side and be able to support the legislation.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister was saying this: There might be some misguided individual-and I am paraphrasing his words-there might be some misguided individual in Canada who would have the effrontery to challenge in the courts of the land some of the edicts which are passed by this government. Now, this supreme, almighty, all-powerful government cannot run the risk that an equally misguided court might conceivably say that this misguided subject was right in his interpretation of the law and that in fact this all-powerful, this omnipotent and benevolent government had exceeded the authority conferred upon it; because of the revulsion it would create 68108-110
Emergency Powers Act in the minds of the whole people of Canada to see this omnipotent and benevolent government challenged in the courts and turned down by the courts, why, we have to make assurance doubly sure that the courts can never find the government of Canada at fault. And therefore we will take not just the powers we need but we will take twice, nay thrice as many powers as we need and thus we will assure that no citizen who might ever be misguided enough, in his ignorance, to challenge the edict of the government need ever fear that in fact that misguided attempt would be upheld by the courts. And so he says: It is therefore important to have the language so broad that the courts will not say: You have gone beyond what parliament authorized you to do.
Mr. Speaker, what a principle! What a principle for a Prime Minister who says, and says with all the solemnity of his office: I uphold the principles of responsible government. There was never a more dangerous, more vicious principle enunciated, particularly, Mr. Speaker, when the government is asking parliament to hand over to the executive all its responsibilities, and with them all the safeguards which normally protect the citizen, which existed heretofore, and existed only as a result of the fact that parliament can call the executive to account.

Emergency Powers Act 1951, was so uncertain that there might be some justification tor taking emergency powers.

Then the Prime Minister in 1952 again favoured us with a speech-somewhat shorter than he made in 1951, but still a speech. There he took the opposite tack to the one he took in 1951. Yes, so he walks out. In 1951 he told us the government was taking powers greater than it would ever need. In 1952 it was quite different. In 1952 the poor government, he says, far from seeking to impose upon, parliament and the people powers away beyond what is proper, does just the opposite, and saddles itself with responsibilities far greater than it had before. Here is what the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 2558 of Hansard for May 26, 1952:
In reality the purpose-
That is, the purpose of the legislation, -was to increase the responsibility of the government, subject to the control of parliament, to meet such emergencies as it might suddenly become necessary to deal with in order to preserve the peace, order and good government of the country in the then threatening international situation. It was not that the government wanted greater powers. It was passed because it was deemed to be a wise precaution to make it the responsibility of the government to act quickly if and when prompt action might be necessary, and to be able to take such action without proclaiming the more sweeping War Measures Act unless it became absolutely necessary to put that act into operation.

Now I am sure that you, sir, and my hon. friend opposite who interrupts, and all the rest of us, will have great sympathy with the government because, poor creatures that they are, they have saddled themselves with this responsibility far beyond anything that they might ever have believed it was necessary they should assume.
I would be interested, I would be pleased, and my constituents would be pleased, and the constituents of every hon. member in the house would be pleased, to relieve the government of those responsibilities.

(a)	control and suppression of maps, plans and photographs;
(b)	control of communications and means of communication;

(d)	transportation by land, air or water and the control of the transport of persons and things;

It is a very important point to have settled, and it does not seem to have been settled definitely by the Speaker in his ruling of June, 1952. When I refer back to 1951, at which time a similar resolution was introduced for the first time, I find that we had a debate lasting a day without any controversy on the point at all. On February 20, 1951, the Prime Minister moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to empower the governor in council to do and authorize such acts and things-*
This resolution that we are supposed to consider in committee is only an extension of the act that followed as a result of the consideration of that resolution in 1951. I cannot see how the Minister of Justice can be right tonight and the Prime Minister right on February 20, 1951. One of them must be wrong. The procedure is not the same.
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West).l

The procedure being followed now is different, and I am inclined to think the Prime Minister was right in 1951, and that this has been the practice that has generally been followed.
